QF.id: AIFM CII Legal Documents and Negotiations_10

question.text: To avoid breaching fiduciary duty to other investors while granting differential rights to large LPs via side letters, most investment managers follow which drafting practice?

answer.text: They refuse to enter into any side letter, regardless of LP size.
They file each side letter individually with SEBI within 7 days of execution.
They create a separate class of units with differential rights, issued to large investors.
They get written consent from every existing LP before executing any side letter.

explanation.text: The Logic: The chapter notes that to avoid fiduciary breach while still accommodating large-LP differential rights, most managers create a SEPARATE CLASS OF UNITS with differential rights, issued to those large investors. This keeps class-level terms transparent, documented in the PPM, and free of the 'preference by concealment' risk of bilateral side letters. The Trap: Refusing all side letters is commercially impractical for anchor LPs. There is no 7-day SEBI filing requirement for every side letter. Universal existing-LP consent is not a required drafting mechanism — that would be operationally unworkable. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C covers side-letter architecture in the same way. XXI-B Portfolio Manager has no class-of-units concept because PMS is per-client account. Manager's Pro-Tip: Design class-A/class-B at fund launch itself with a fee grid tied to commitment tiers (₹10cr, ₹50cr, ₹100cr, ₹250cr+). Retro-fitting classes after first close is legally messy and invites MFN claims.
